title: THE PRISONER WHO BECAME A WITNESS
paragraphs: THE PRISONER WHO BECAME A WITNESS
The chains rattled every time he moved.
Cold iron around bruised wrists. A damp cell. The smell of stone, sweat, and hopelessness lingering in the darkness.
Most people assume prison begins when a door closes.
Others live inside the human heart.
The Bible is filled with prisoners.
Joseph was thrown into an Egyptian dungeon.
Jeremiah was lowered into a muddy cistern.
John the Baptist sat in Herod’s prison awaiting execution.
Yet among all these stories stands one that feels surprisingly familiar to modern readers—not because of iron bars, but because of the scandal attached to the prisoner.
A man whose past should have disqualified him.
A man whose reputation should have buried him.
A man who became one of history’s greatest witnesses.
And before he became an apostle, he was known as Saul.
The man who once hunted Christians became one.
The man who approved executions would one day preach the very gospel he tried to destroy.
And in his story, countless souls discover their own.
The first time we meet Saul, blood stains the scene.
Acts 7 records the martyrdom of Stephen, the first Christian martyr.
As stones crashed against Stephen’s body, witnesses laid their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul.
The Greek text uses the word συνευδοκέω (syneudokeō), meaning to fully consent, approve, or take pleasure in agreement.
Saul was not a passive observer.
He believed he was serving God.
He believed he was protecting truth.
Yet sincerity does not guarantee righteousness.
Many of us have wounds created by things we were convinced were right.
Like Saul, we often discover that being convinced is not the same as being correct.
The scandal of Saul’s story is not merely what he did.
The scandal is what Jesus did with him afterward.
On the road to Damascus, everything changed.
Acts 9 describes a blinding light from heaven.
“Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting Me?”
The risen Christ did not ask why Saul persecuted Christians.
Jesus identified so closely with His people that persecuting them was persecuting Him.
“Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting Me?”
The word διώκεις (diōkeis) means to pursue, chase, hunt down, or persecute relentlessly.
Saul thought he was chasing believers.
In reality, he was fighting against God Himself.
And suddenly the hunter became the one being pursued.
This is the mystery of grace.
Long before Saul sought Christ, Christ sought Saul.
Long before Saul surrendered, Jesus confronted him.
Long before Saul changed, God had already written a different ending.
That truth alone has rescued countless believers from despair.
Because if grace could reach Saul, grace can reach anyone.
The Hebrew Scriptures repeatedly reveal a God who pursues people long before they pursue Him.
When Adam hid among the trees, God asked, “Where are you?”
When Jonah fled toward Tarshish, God sent a storm.
When Peter denied Christ, Jesus restored him.
When Saul hunted Christians, Jesus met him on the road.
The prisoner never unlocks the cell.
For many readers, the prison is not physical.
The memory of something done years ago that still whispers accusations in the middle of the night.
The enemy loves to convince believers that forgiveness has limits.
Yet Scripture keeps presenting evidence to the contrary.
Notice what he does not say.
He does not minimize his sin.
He does not pretend his past was misunderstood.
This is why Paul never stopped talking about his past.
Not because he was trapped by it.
Because he had been freed from it.
Years later, another prison cell would become the setting for one of the most remarkable demonstrations of Christian hope.
The former persecutor now suffered persecution himself.
The former jailer became the jailed.
The former hunter became the hunted.
Yet his letters from prison overflow with joy.
Philippians, often called the Epistle of Joy, was written during imprisonment.
Because freedom and confinement are not always opposites.
A person can walk freely through city streets while imprisoned by fear.
Another can sit behind bars while liberated by Christ.
Paul understood something the world rarely understands.
The deepest freedom is not external.
Jesus taught this long before Paul wrote it.
“So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.”
The Greek phrase is ὄντως ἐλεύθεροι (ontōs eleutheroi).
Freedom at the deepest level of existence.
Freedom from trying to earn what God already gives through Christ.
This is the heartbeat of the gospel.
The world often defines people by their worst moment.
The gospel defines people by Christ’s finished work.
The world says, “Look what you did.”
Perhaps that is why Paul’s life continues to resonate across centuries.
Most readers see themselves somewhere in his journey.
But as someone who has failed.
Someone who wonders whether God could really use them.
Someone who fears that yesterday’s mistakes have permanently shaped tomorrow.
The cross answers it even louder.
At Calvary, Jesus bore not only our sins but also our shame.
“Surely He has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows.”
The Hebrew word for “borne” is נָשָׂא (nasa’).
Christ carried what was crushing us.
He entered our prison so we could enter His freedom.
The resurrection became Heaven’s declaration that the debt was fully paid.
This is why Christianity is ultimately not a story about good people becoming better.
It is a story about dead people becoming alive.
Even now, someone reading these words may feel trapped by a chapter they wish had never happened.
The enemy wants that chapter to become your identity.
Jesus wants it to become part of your testimony.
The same God who met Saul on the Damascus road still meets people in unexpected places.
And yes, sometimes even in the middle of scandal.
Because grace specializes in places where hope appears impossible.
That is the story of Scripture from Genesis to Revelation.
If this story stirred something in your heart, be honest.
The chapter that shames you today may become the testimony that leads someone else to Jesus tomorrow.
